Liao Ling (Twill Waved Silk) written by the famous Tang dynasty (618- 907 CE) poet Bai Juyi (722- 846 CE) and the handscroll Dao Lian Tu (Court Ladies Preparing Newly Woven Silk) painted by Zhang Xian (713- 55 CE). Silk fabrics such as juan (plain tabby silk) and ling were also used as a medium for paintings and calligraphy, wrappers and mounting materials. 
Beginning in the Song dynasty (960- 1279) and flourishing into the Qing (1644- 1911), craftsmen took up shutters and needles as their brushes and silk threads as their pigments for creating woven and embroidered pictorial and calligraphic works. For the hands of weavers and embroiderers, the weft-woven silk tapestry (kezi) and embroidery (cizhi) evolved into an art form—a beautiful combination of painting, calligraphy and hand weaving or embroidery. These works were created for aesthetic appreciation, beyond their traditional role as clothing and decorative items. Unlike traditional Chinese painting and calligraphy which emphasize tying (artistic conception)—the expression of an artist's ideals and values—pictorial and calligraphic silk tapestry and embroidery rely on the vivid and life- like depiction of images and text through a range of weaving and embroidery techniques. Together, their interdisciplinary nature offers these silk works a unique and unbroken place in Chinese visual culture. 
## Silk tapestry and embroidery: techniques and origins 
Silk refers to the long filament produced by silkworms that are fed exclusively on mulberry leaves. The material is lustrous, elastic, soft and thin, with a diameter of only 0.9 millimetres. Up to 1,000 metres of silk can be reeled from a single cocoon. The natural gaps in the filament mean that silk is well-ventilated and absorbent, making it a perfect material for clothing. Silk has been used historically in a diverse range of fabrics that can be classified according to structure (plain weave, twill- weave, satin- weave, gauze and rug (velvet)), surface pattern, colour and origin. 
Woven on small looms, Chinese silk tapestry is a type of handwoven textile that employs a technique known as tongjing daunwei ('continuous warp and broken weft'). Small shutters carrying polychrome wefts move back and forth across the warp threads within a defined pattern. Unlike other woven textiles created in a plain weave, weft threads in a silk tapestry do not run across the entirety of the fabric. The use of coloured weft threads and patterns woven in other silk fabrics, such as brocade, are relatively limited, or else are reserved for the continuous run of weft threads. The tapestry weavers could easily and freely employ an endless number of coloured wefts that create individual patterned segments, resulting in a saw- tooled split between the adjacently coloured weft patterns. From a distance, such splits create a visual effect similar to carving; in fact, Chinese silk tapestry was first known as kezi ('carved silk'), while another homophonic variant for the character ke ('weft- 
woven) was adopted by scholars in the Ming dynasty (1368- 1644) to as to highlight this characteristic weaving technique. (Fig. 1) 
Though the principle of the silk tapestry weave is relatively simple, the production process is extremely time-consuming. Warp threads in raw silk are first stretched onto a wooden loom. 'Weevers then place a jenfen ('cartoon') beneath the warps and use a brush to outline the patterns on the warp threads. Dyed weft threads are inserted into individual small boat-like shuttles, which are then meticulously handwoven into the warp threads to create a polychrome composition. Developed by generations of weavers, the primary techniques include 'go (outlining)' for defining the silhouette of patterns, along with guan ('flinging'), jie ('connecting') and guan ('propelling'). Each technique employs similar tones of polychrome wefts to achieve a gradation of colours. (Fig. 2 & 3) To preserve the silk between the adjacent weft patterns from becoming too large, weavers also employ the dana ('shuttle joining') technique to reduce the spacing. Weft threads of the adjacent patterns are interwoven with the warp threads of the opposite coloured wefts, and when one distance based on the size of the slits as a way to stabilise the weaving structure. 
Unlike kezi silk tapestry, in which warp and weft threads are used to complete a new piece of fabric, embroidery uses needle and thread to decorate a ground fabric, or another medium that can be pierced.
